Core Emit State Behavior

Core Emit State Behavior provides a controlled, observational mechanism for responding to finalized state snapshots after pipeline execution completes. It executes after state commitment and exposure, allowing legacy or convenience callbacks to observe state changes without influencing pipeline execution or state authority.

Emit-State Callback Contract Summary

  • Emit-state callbacks are observational only and must not modify state
  • Emit-state callbacks must not throw or interrupt execution
  • Emit-state callbacks receive the finalized immutable state snapshot
  • Emit-state callbacks execute after state commitment and exposure
  • Callback execution does not affect state commitment or pipeline outcome

The Core Emit State contract guarantees that callback execution is isolated and non-authoritative. Callbacks are invoked only after the state snapshot has been fully committed and exposed through the FeatureCell’s state surfaces. Any failures within callbacks are contained and do not alter committed state or pipeline completion semantics.

Core Emit State Behaviors do not participate in state derivation, state commitment, pipeline control, or scheduling. Their sole responsibility is to provide a compatibility and observation surface for already-finalized state snapshots.

Add-on State Emit Callback Behaviors

In addition to core state commitment and snapshot exposure, FeatureCells may opt into add-on state emit callback behaviors. These behaviors observe the finalized StateSnapshotShape after it has been committed and exposed and may perform supplemental, observational handling such as logging, diagnostics, integration hooks, or compatibility callbacks.

Emit-state callbacks do not replace, suppress, or alter state commitment. They do not derive values, do not influence pipeline control flow, and do not participate in pipeline admission. Their responsibility is limited to observing immutable snapshots that already represent a completed pipeline execution.

Emit-state callbacks exist primarily for convenience and backward compatibility with callback-oriented or imperative codebases. The primary mechanisms for consuming state are .state (synchronous getter; represented as a signal in Angular) and .state$ (reactive observable). Emit-state callbacks should not be relied upon for core application logic.

Fluent emitStates() API

A FeatureCell may declare multiple emit-state callbacks using the fluent .emitStates() API. This API accepts an ordered array of callbacks that are executed sequentially after each state snapshot has been finalized and exposed. Callback registration occurs during FeatureCell initialization.

Emit-state callbacks are strictly observational. They do not return values, do not modify the snapshot, and always yield VAULT_NOOP. An empty emitStates array is ignored and has no effect on pipeline execution.

Engineer-Supplied Emit-State Callbacks

Emit-state callbacks are supplied by engineers during FeatureCell initialization and execute exclusively after the authoritative state snapshot has been committed. Each callback receives the finalized immutable StateSnapshotShape representing pipeline completion.

Callbacks must not throw, must not mutate the snapshot, and must not attempt to resume or interrupt pipeline execution. Any errors raised by callbacks are isolated and do not affect state commitment, state exposure, or downstream observers.

Note

Although multiple emit-state callbacks may be composed, callback logic should remain narrowly scoped and observational. Complex or interdependent callbacks can obscure intent and complicate state-change analysis. Emit-state callbacks are most effective when limited to diagnostics, transitional compatibility, or integration side effects.

Diagrams
Configuration

Emit-state callbacks are configured separately from core state commitment and snapshot exposure. When declared, the FeatureCell registers a core emit-state behavior that executes after the state snapshot has been finalized, committed, and exposed through the standard state surfaces. Emit-state callbacks are attached exclusively through the fluent .emitStates() API during FeatureCell initialization.

Emit-state callbacks are optional and strictly observational. They do not participate in state derivation, do not modify the committed state snapshot, and do not influence pipeline control or execution. Callback execution is isolated, and any failures within callbacks do not affect state commitment, state exposure, or downstream observers.

State Emit Patterns

Emit-state callbacks permit side effects, but they execute only after a state snapshot has been finalized and committed by the State stage. Emit-state callbacks must not influence pipeline execution, must not modify the committed snapshot, and must not be used as an alternative to consuming .state or .state$.

Emit-state callbacks are registered through the fluent .emitStates() API and are invoked sequentially for each committed state snapshot. The categories below describe supported and discouraged callback patterns, ordered from most to least preferred.

Category A: Pure / Context-Free Functions (Recommended)

Pure emit-state callbacks depend only on their input snapshot and perform deterministic, observational side effects. They do not reference instance context and do not close over mutable external state.

This is the safest and most reusable emit-state callback form.

Example 1: Pure Emit-State Callback

{{`employeeCell.emitStates(
  [
    (snapshot: StateSnapshotShape<Employee[]>) => {
      console.info('State committed');
      console.info('isLoading:', snapshot.isLoading);
      console.info('hasValue:', snapshot.hasValue);
      console.info('value:', snapshot.value);
      console.info('error:', snapshot.error);
    }
  ]
).initialize();`}}

Example 2: Factory-Generated Pure Emit-State Callback

{{`export function createStateLogger(label: string) {
  return (snapshot: StateSnapshotShape<Employee[]>) => {
    console.info(label, 'hasValue=', snapshot.hasValue, 'isLoading=', snapshot.isLoading);
  };
}

employeeCell.emitStates(
  [
    createStateLogger('EmployeeCell')
  ]
).initialize();`}}

Category B: Instance-Aware but Correctly Bound Callbacks (Acceptable)

Emit-state callbacks may reference instance-owned configuration when properly bound. These callbacks remain deterministic per FeatureCell instance and must not be shared across FeatureCells.

Example 3: Arrow Function Using Instance State

{{`readonly prefix = '[Employee State]';

readonly logState = (snapshot: StateSnapshotShape<Employee[]>) => {
  console.info(this.prefix, snapshot.hasValue ? 'value present' : 'no value');
};

employeeCell.emitStates(
  [this.logState]
).initialize();`}}

Example 4: Bound Instance Method

{{`public logState(snapshot: StateSnapshotShape<Employee[]>) {
  console.info('Committed snapshot value:', snapshot.value);
}

employeeCell.emitStates(
  [this.logState.bind(this)]
).initialize();`}}

Category C: Delegating Callbacks

Emit-state callbacks may delegate work to helper functions as long as delegation remains observational and does not rely on external mutable state.

Example 5: Delegated Emit-State Logging

{{`function logSnapshot(snapshot: StateSnapshotShape<Employee[]>) {
  console.info('Snapshot committed. hasValue=', snapshot.hasValue);
}

employeeCell.emitStates(
  [
    (snapshot: StateSnapshotShape<Employee[]>) => logSnapshot(snapshot)
  ]
).initialize();`}}

Category D: Inline Lambda Callbacks (Allowed, Use Sparingly)

Inline callbacks are allowed but should remain trivial. Inline lambdas make it easy to accidentally introduce hidden coupling or complex logic.

Example 6: Inline Conditional Emit-State Callback

{{`employeeCell.emitStates(
  [
    (snapshot: StateSnapshotShape<Employee[]>) => {
      if (snapshot.error) {
        console.info('State committed with error:', snapshot.error.message);
      }
    }
  ]
).initialize();`}}
State Emit Anti-Patterns

Emit-state callbacks are observational hooks. They exist solely to observe finalized state snapshots after state commitment. They must not influence pipeline execution, must not modify committed state, and must not be treated as an alternative to consuming .state or .state$.

Misuse of emit-state callbacks can introduce hidden coupling, incorrect assumptions about pipeline guarantees, or subtle state visibility bugs.

Common Anti-Patterns

  • Mutating the committed state snapshot
  • Attempting to derive, replace, or “fix” state values
  • Embedding business logic or decision-making
  • Performing long-running, blocking, or asynchronous work
  • Depending on external mutable or shared state
  • Assuming emit-state callbacks influence pipeline flow or recovery

Violations in emit-state callbacks are not always mechanically detectable. Issues typically surface as subtle bugs, degraded observability, or incorrect mental models of state finalization.

Example: Discouraged Mutation Inside an Emit-State Callback

{{`employeeCell.emitStates(
  [
    (snapshot: StateSnapshotShape<Employee[]>) => {
      // ❌ Mutating the finalized state snapshot
      snapshot.value = [];
      snapshot.hasValue = false;
      console.info('Modified snapshot value:', snapshot.value);
    }
  ]
).initialize();

// ❌ Violates the emit-state contract: snapshots are immutable and authoritative`}}

Even if such mutation appears to have an effect locally, it violates pipeline guarantees. Emit-state callbacks must treat the state snapshot as immutable, authoritative, and already finalized.

State Emit Callback Summary

State Emit Callback Comparison

The following table summarizes the practical differences between the state emit callback styles demonstrated above. While all valid examples may execute correctly, they differ in reusability, testability, and long-term safety when observing finalized state snapshots.

State Emit Callback Characteristics
Dimension Examples 1 / 2
Pure / Factory Callbacks 		Examples 3 / 4
Instance-Bound Callbacks 		Example 5
Delegating Callback 		Example 6
Inline Lambda
Purity ✅ ⚠️ Instance-scoped ⚠️ Delegate-dependent ⚠️
Determinism ✅ ⚠️ Per FeatureCell ⚠️ Delegate-dependent ⚠️
Safety for State Emission ✅ ✅ ⚠️ ⚠️
Reusability High Medium Medium Low
Testability High Medium Medium Lower
Risk of Accidental Closure Low Low Medium High
Intended Lifespan Long-lived Instance-limited Contextual Ephemeral
Recommended Usage Preferred Acceptable Use with care Use sparingly

Summary Rule

Any state emit callback must either be referentially transparent or explicitly instance-scoped and bound. Emit-state callbacks must treat the received state snapshot as immutable and authoritative and must not assume they influence state commitment, pipeline execution, or downstream visibility.

Examples

Example 1: Register a State Emit Callback

{{`// app.config.ts

export const appConfig: ApplicationConfig = {
  providers: [
    provideVault({ logLevel: 'off' }),

    provideFeatureCell(
      EmployeeService
      {
        key: 'employees',
        initialState: [],
      },
      [
        // **Important**
        // State emit callbacks are not registered as part of the
        // FeatureCell's declarative configuration.
      ],
      [
        // opt-in Controllers
      ]
    )
  ]
};

// bank-employee.service.ts

import { Injectable } from '@angular/core';
import { FeatureCell, injectVault } from '@sdux-vault/angular';
import { Employee } from './employee.shape';

@FeatureCell`}}<Employee[]>{{`('employees')
@Injectable({ providedIn: 'root' })
export class EmployeeService {
  readonly vault = injectVault`}}<Employee[]>{{`(EmployeeService);

  constructor() {
    this.vault
      .emitStates(
        [
          (snapshot) => {
            // Observational side effect only
            console.info('Employees snapshot emitted');
            console.info('Current value:', snapshot.value);
            console.info('Loading:', snapshot.isLoading);
          }
        ]
      )
      .initialize();
  }
}`}}
 
{{`export const employeeCell = FeatureCell`}}<Employee[]>{{`(
  {
    key: 'employees',
    initialState: [],
  },
  [
    // **Important**
    // State emit callbacks are not part of declarative configuration.
  ],
  [
    // opt-in Controllers
  ]
);

// Register a state emit callback during initialization
employeeCell
  .emitStates(
    [
      (snapshot) => {
        console.info('Employees snapshot emitted');
        console.info('Value:', snapshot.value);
        console.info('Has value:', snapshot.hasValue);
      }
    ]
  )
  .initialize();`}}

Example 2: Async State Emit Callback (Remote Logging)

{{`// bank-employee.service.ts

@Injectable({ providedIn: 'root' })
export class EmployeeService {
  readonly vault = injectVault`}}<Employee[]>{{`(EmployeeService);

  constructor() {
    this.vault
      .emitStates(
        [
          async (snapshot) => {
            await logStateToApi({
              feature: 'employees',
              value: snapshot.value,
              isLoading: snapshot.isLoading,
              hasValue: snapshot.hasValue,
            });
          }
        ]
      )
      .initialize();
  }
}

async function logStateToApi(payload: {
  feature: string;
  value: unknown;
  isLoading: boolean;
  hasValue: boolean;
}): Promise`}}<void>{{` {
  await fetch('/api/logs/state', {
    method: 'POST',
    headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
    body: JSON.stringify(payload),
  });
}`}}
 
{{`async function logState(payload: {
  feature: string;
  value: unknown;
}) {
  await fetch('/api/logs/state', {
    method: 'POST',
    headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
    body: JSON.stringify(payload),
  });
}

employeeCell
  .emitStates(
    [
      async (snapshot) => {
        await logState({
          feature: 'employees',
          value: snapshot.value,
        });
      }
    ]
  )
  .initialize();`}}
